title: Photography and illustration direction for a young brand
excerpt: Brand photography direction is a decision about subject, crop, and what you will not show. A young brand gets consistency from those limits, not from more pictures.
alt: Blue and orange ink blooming through water. The mixing color fits a piece about choosing a visual direction and the things you will not show.
caption: Direction is a limit on color, subject, and crop. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a photography direction include?
faqs.answer: Name the subject, the crop, the light, and a short list of things you will not show. Three example frames are more useful than a paragraph of mood words. If a new photo cannot be judged against the examples, the direction is still a vibe.

faqs.question: When should a young brand use illustration instead of photography?
faqs.answer: Use illustration when the product is invisible, when you do not yet have real scenes to photograph, or when a diagram will explain more than a picture of a laptop. Use photography when the object, the place, or the material is the point. Mixing both is fine if they share a palette and a level of detail.

faqs.question: How many images does a first site need?
faqs.answer: Fewer than a stock library suggests. A homepage can be honest with a handful of frames that follow one crop and one subject. A dozen unrelated photos look busier and less like a brand. Add images when a page has a new job, not when a section feels empty.

markdown:
Brand photography direction is a decision about subject, crop, and what you will not show. A young brand does not need a large library. It needs a rule strict enough that the next picture belongs with the last one. Without the rule, every section of the site becomes a different company that happened to share a logo.

Direction is not a mood board of other people's work with the nouns swapped. It is a short brief you can hand to a photographer, an illustrator, or yourself. Subject. Crop. Light. The things that are out.

## Subject

Decide what the pictures are of. The object you sell. The material it is made from. The place it is used. The people, if people are truly part of the offer and you can photograph them with their knowledge. A brand that cannot answer this will fill the homepage with laptops, handshakes, and plants, because those are what stock libraries offer to everyone.

Wabisabi is a public example of a calm, tactile visual world. The lesson to take is not a specific photo. It is that a brand site can choose quiet and touch, and then refuse the loud default. A community sports brand would choose a different subject and still be disciplined. The discipline is the direction. The subject is yours.

Write the subject as a noun you can point at. Hands at a bench. A folded garment. A single tool on a plain surface. If the noun is innovation or community, you do not have a subject yet. You have a theme, and themes produce generic pictures.

## Crop, light, and color

Pick a crop and stay with it. Tight on the material, or a wider frame that includes the room, but not both at random. Mixed crops in one grid make a shop or a portfolio look unfinished, even when each photo is good. The eye reads the inconsistency before it reads the quality.

Pick a light. Window light with soft shadow. Even light and almost no shadow. Hard sun. One of these, across the set. A set that jumps from flash to candlelight looks like it was gathered, not directed.

Color in the photograph should be able to sit next to the brand colors without a fight. That does not mean the photo is tinted to the accent. It means you do not introduce a second palette by accident, a neon sign in a quiet brand, a brown filter on a brand that is trying to look precise. If the picture needs a filter to belong, the picture is the wrong picture.

Illustration follows the same limits. One line weight or one texture. A palette taken from the brand colors, not from the default swatches in the tool. A subject matter that matches the photographs if both appear on the same site. A flat character set next to documentary photos will look like two vendors delivered the page.

## What you will not show

The refusal is the part that makes a direction usable. Write it down.

- No fake dashboards hovering over a desk.
- No crowds looking at a laptop and laughing.
- No illustrations of puzzles, rockets, and lightbulbs unless the product is literally one of those.
- No crop that cuts a person's face in a way you would not tolerate in a portrait.

Your list should be specific to the feeling you already refused when the identity was only a name. A serious tool refuses jokes in the pictures. A craft brand refuses glossy, context-free product renders if the point is the hand. A calm brand refuses high-contrast clutter in the background.

The refusal also covers how people are depicted, if they appear. Do not use a customer's face without a real yes. Do not invent a diverse team you do not have. A direction that depends on fiction will embarrass you the moment a buyer visits the actual room.

## Alt text is part of the direction

Every image on the site needs a text alternative that describes what is in the frame. The W3C's [WCAG 2 overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) treats web content as text, images, and the code that presents them, under principles that begin with perceivable. A photograph that carries meaning has to be perceivable by someone who does not see it. Alt text that repeats the keyword, or that says image of homepage, fails the person and fails the direction.

Write the alt as a caption would, in the brand's sentences. A folded linen shirt on a pale wood shelf. Not: best ecommerce lifestyle photography for modern brands. The second line is an advertisement stuffed into an accessibility field. The first line is the picture.

Decorative marks can have empty alt text. A hero that explains the product cannot. Decide which is which when you choose the image, not after launch.

## How to brief a small shoot

A first shoot can be a morning. Bring the product, the surface, and three reference frames that already match the crop and the light. Tell the photographer the refusals before you tell them to be creative. Creativity inside a limit is how you get a set. Creativity without a limit is how you get twelve tests and no system.

Review the selects against the brief, not against which frame is the most dramatic. The dramatic frame is often the one that breaks the crop or introduces a color you did not allow. Keep a short contact sheet of approved frames in the same place as the logo files. The next person to add a picture should match the sheet.

Illustration briefs are the same shape. A sentence of subject, a sentence of how it is drawn, and a sentence of what is out. Ask for one sample before a set. Approve the sample in writing. A set drawn in the wrong texture is a week you do not get back.

Use fewer images than you think. A page with one honest photograph and real type will look more like a brand than a page tiled with unrelated stock. Empty space is not a failure of direction. It is often the direction working.

When the pictures are products in a grid, the crop rules get even stricter. [Photography, crop, and the product grid](/blog/photography-and-the-product-grid) is the next piece if you are shooting for a shop rather than a story.

When you want the visual direction made with the site, see [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The public projects show how a point of view survives once it is on a page.
